newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: African leaders back Kabila on massacre probe.
newsitem.headline: African leaders back Kabila on massacre probe.

text.p: Eight African leaders rallied behind Laurent Kabila on Sunday, backing his call that a U.N. massacre investigation in the former Zaire be extended beyond the seven-month revolt that brought him to power.

The heads of state of Uganda, Rwanda, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Namibia, Mozambique, Eritrea and Central African Republic pledged their support for Kabila at the one-day summit and for his efforts to rebuild Africa's third largest nation.

Their final statement after a meeting of over three hours "noted with dismay" what they called a campaign of vilification against Kabila and the people of the renamed Democratic Republic of the Congo and against certain of its neighbours.

"They welcome the setting up of the U.N. commission to investigate alleged violations of human rights in the Congo. The leaders reiterate the demand for a neutral and independent commission," the statement said.
"They supported the Congo's demand for widening the scope to include crimes committed since 1993 and they offered their active participation in this investigation."
Kabila and his forces toppled veteran dictator Mobutu Sese Seko in May. Kabila has banned political activity and accorded himself, as president, wide-ranging powers.

The U.N. set up the investigation to look into allegations that Kabila's fighters or their Rwandan and other Tutsi allies killed Rwandan Hutu refugees during their march across Zaire. Kabila dismisses talk of massacres.
The refugees were among the rump of over a million Rwandan Hutus who fled to Zaire fearing reprisals after the 1994 genocide by Hutu hardliners of minority Tutsis. Most returned home in December.
The statement said that the leaders "noted with appreciation the total repatriation of the few remaining refugees scattered in various parts of the Congo".
U.N. relief officials estimate that as many as 200,000 Hutus have gone missing in the former Zaire and may be living in forests there or worse.

Kabila's government has already persuaded the U.N. to change the head of the investigation. It accused Chilean human rights lawyer Roberto Garreton of bias. Garreton has published reports accusing Kabila's forces and their allies of killings.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan backed Garreton but agreed to switch him in the interests of the investigation going ahead. Human Rights watchdog Amnesty International has urged to U.N. to act firmly on the investigation.

Kabila took over a country which is potentially one of Africa's richest but has been drained by three decades of corruption and administrative chaos. His Congo has a wealth of minerals, rich farmland and huge hydro-electric potential.

The statements said that the leaders affirmed "unequivocal support" for Kabila and the people of his Congo "in their efforts to establish sound administration, economic recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction of their country as well as their efforts consolidating their revolution".
They urged African leaders and the international community to follow suit.
Zimbabwe's President Robert Mugabe is chairman of the Organisation of African Unity. Uganda's Yoweri Museveni has been a staunch supporter of the revolt that toppled Mobutu.
